-Fathers O'Neill and Dion wish to know how elections are bought and how votes are bartered for pieces of silver and television sets, I suggest to them that they follow the campaign of the hon. member for Temiscouata when he runs in the next election. Those are things which should not be left to the imagination of the people. Those are the facts that deserve to be known. We

did not come here to be treated in the manner this Liberal party has seen fit to treat us. We came here to do a job, and that is all we want to do. As I said, we would be the first to congratulate you if you would do your job. It is the same old game with the Liberals of divide and conquer; playing on the ignorance of people. Lie and tell more lies, and that is the way they will do in the future, too.
I know that when I ran for election the hon. member for Gloucester, Hot Shot as his Liberal friends call him, went about saying: "If you vote for Van Horne you will lose your old age pensions and family allowances". When I spoke in the house just after I came here and asked for an increase in family allowances to compensate for the increases in the cost of living since 1945, and increases of $20 in old age pensions, he was the first man and the only man who got up and berated me and opposed me for asking for these increases. Just where are we going with this type of administration?
Possibly many of you believe I should refer to the hon. member for Charlotte, whom I see across the way, as the result of his remarks about our bellyaching for the things we need in the maritime provinces. Let me tell him that our bellyaching did not do much good. We are going to have to keep on bellyaching in order to get the things we need in the maritime provinces. If they were to suddenly solve only a few of our problems, it would be a help.
Just let me proceed by mentioning the tight money policy. If inflation exists in this country it is because of the government's monetary policy over the last 20 years. The worth of our dollar has gone down to 53.5 cents since 1939. This policy is further crippling the already limping economy of the maritime provinces. We have a recent statement from Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, that further restrictions are in the offing.
Now, inflation does not exist in the mari-times. We are all agreed on this point. The crying need of the maritimes is for expanded credit and low interest rates. Easy money and more money are the urgent necessities of the maritime provinces if we are to improve the economy of that region. We are also all agreed on this point. I am sure the Minister of Public Works would be the first to admit it, and so would the Minister of Labour.
It is axiomatic that our economic situation in the maritime provinces is the complete reverse of the situation which may exist in central Canada. Our provinces, cities, villages

and towns, our small businessmen and our new ventures need money if we are to overcome the need for one-way tickets to central Canada. I am wondering if, in the coming election to be fought by the Liberals in the maritimes, they are going to use the slogan, "Vote Liberal and get a one-way ticket". This would be a fine accomplishment indeed to show for 20 years of misrule.
Let me tell you how this migration takes place in my riding, because I know whereof I speak. You go into a house in Madawaska county and you will find the father, mother and possibly one son or a daughter who have succeeded in getting work in the pulp mills. All the other sons and daughters are in Hartford, Connecticut. Half of my Madawaska constituents are in Hartford, Connecticut. The migration from other areas is to different places. From Atholville, where 1 went to school, the people go to Niagara Fails; from Campbellton they go to Toronto; from Edmundston they go to Seven Islands-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They all left after you were elected.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just a second; that remark shows the puerile mind of some of the Liberals. That migration has been going on for years and years and it is time it stopped. I do not blame it all on the Liberal party; the blame must be shared by all gov-vernments since confederation, because we have never received a just deal in the maritime provinces since confederation. The migration keeps on. I was talking to one bishop some time ago and he said that parishes are emptying. That is the situation. How can traditions be maintained and how can families be united if they are to be forever torn asunder and driven away like nomads into the desert, driven from our homes by the same economic conditions that yesteryear drove our forefathers from the shores of Europe in great numbers?
Our problems today are far too serious to permit the entrance into this debate of petty Liberal politics. In order to cure inflation which might exist in central Canada the government pursues and continues the dictatorial policy of prohibitively high interest rates and scarce money in all parts of Canada. This policy is applied right across the board. The government says, when too many dollars are chasing too few goods, let us cut down and then we shall have fewer dollars with which to buy the goods.
I am informed that when Mr. Coyne forced his views upon the cabinet he did so without calling in or consulting the presidents of
30, 1957
The Budget-Mr. Van Horne our other banks, as was the habit of Mr. Graham Towers. In other words, the dictatorship which is so obvious in the cabinet is spreading to other government departments and crown corporations. The other school of economists affirms that the real cure for inflation, if it exists anywhere in Canada, is greater productivity. Let the dollars catch the goods they are chasing in a quantity sufficient to keep the prices down.
In other words inflation exists because of too few goods. The cure is more goods, more production, more turnout per unit of workmanship by better tools and equipment. As one of the elder Liberal statesmen of New Brunswick, Senator Neil McLean of Saint John, made clear on many occasions, and how true it is, the tight money prevents urgently needed expansion designed for greater production. These things are scuttled because of the tight money policy. Only the very rich companies can expand, and the smaller or normal industries are simply out in the cold, forced to get along without financing or go bankrupt, and many of them are on the verge of bankruptcy. As one eminent elder statesman said, if it seeks to make itself more efficient through scientific means its hands are tied by an out-dated monetary system, which has one quack monetary cure-all for everything, sound or unsound, namely high interest rates. High interest rates and scarce money, jumping jack interest rates.
The hon. member for Gloucester, my friend or rather my friendly enemy, or as some Liberal colleagues call him, Hot Shot, is well aware, because it was reproduced in full newspaper pages of the children in his own riding, as in mine, burning to death around a kitchen stove because they have to live in tar-paper shacks. Mr. Speaker, tobacco road conditions exist in his riding as in mine. The fact is that many of our people are ill-housed, ill-fed and ill-clothed, and as long as I serve as their representative, the representative of all my people, I shall protest against it; make no mistake about that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will not be long.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just a minute. Whoever runs on the Conservative ticket in my riding will win with a greater majority than has ever been seen in the past. Let me pull no punches. These are conditions that deserve attention. The National Housing Act does not meet our needs. I would like the Minister of Public Works, who is sitting across the floor from me now, to understand that we are not advancing these things from any partisan point of view; but if only he could go

The Budget-Mr. Van Horne down to the United States-I presume he has been there

and see how the national housing act in the United States is providing homes for the people of that country, which we are not getting in Canada under the regulations-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not as good an act as ours.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, no, sir; 4 per cent on a $10,000 house is all that is required as a down payment, and that includes many items in the kitchen such as a stove, a refrigerator and, in some cases, even a television set. If our people in Canada could get a house for $400 down our housing problem would be practically solved.
There is no doubt that at the moment it does cost too much to own a home. You know, sir, and the Minister of Public Works knows as well, that in 1954 Central Mortgage and Housing cleared something over $14 million; in 1955 they had a profit on their operations of over $16 million, and that is after they paid the costs of maintaining the big cow palace they have out there as headquarters. I have not the figures for their last year of operation, but I am sure the profit would be as much.
It would not cost the government of this country 5 cents to provide proper homes for the people of this country, so they would not be forced to live in tar-paper shacks with the danger of having their children burned to death around a kitchen stove in winter. I had that happen in my riding last year and the hon. member for Gloucester had it happen in his riding this year. Let us make no mistake about these things. To have to pay $3,000, $4,000 and $5,000 as a down payment on a house is simply placing housing beyond the means of many people in Canada, many people who cannot even afford to pay the high rents charged in the larger centres.
In my area housing is just a farce. I made a survey in one town last year, and found that out of 100 people who were interested in buying a house not one was able to find the down payment of almost $3,000 required on a $12,000 house. Those are facts which you have to consider. Those 100 people were denied the right to occupy a house. These are things which deserve the attention of this government. On a per capita basis Canada has more land, more sea, more fisheries resources, a greater capacity to produce goods and services than any other country in the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And more houses.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Our people are still being burned to death because they have to live in

tar-paper shacks. That is a fact. Every Canadian is potentially the wealthiest person in the world. On the one hand we have this unlimited wealth represented by our minerals, our forests, our ability to produce all kinds of goods, and on the other hand we have 15 million Canadian people. In between is wedged the government, which is preventing this wealth from reaching the people.
I do not know all the reasons, but I am sure lack of foresight and indifference are two of the main reasons. One of the main responsibilities of any government in any country is to take measures, including the changing of outdated and inefficient monetary systems so the potential wealth of the country can be translated into greater production of goods and services for all the people. The stark poverty that we see in northern New Brunswick should never exist in this country. But it does exist and will continue to exist as long as the government pursues its present policies.
The first duty of the government is to put the basic wealth of the country into the hands of the people in a way that will permit Canada to be developed and in such a way that our people can use it. If the wealth of Canada were properly controlled we would not have to go to the United States to borrow money to develop hydro projects like Beechwood. If the Canadian government does not believe in the right of Canadians to credit and money and a share of the wealth of Canada it is high time we did away with such a government. This is especially so when we realize that our neighbours to the south are anxious to provide this credit at a much lower rate and on better terms.
The government's job is to translate our existing wealth in the form of our mines, our fish, our agricultural products and our manufactured goods into homes, food and clothing and the provision of opportunity and security for all our people so they may all be well housed, well fed and well clothed. That is the problem. I presume that is why I was sent here in the first place. Our people were tired of putting up with a government which did not pay attention to these problems.
The Minister of Public Works cannot convince me that he is taking measures to remove the sticks that are in the wheels in regard to housing. If the minister would just understand that our people cannot afford to make a down payment of $3,000 I am sure we would be a long way toward solving the housing problem. The situation may

change with the next election; the people may realize that it is time for a new government.
I should like to refer now to the Department of Transport. When I was running for election down home the Minister of Transport ran all over my riding trying to pick up votes for the Liberal candidate. I do not blame him for doing this, although he did not succeed very well. He went down to the wharf in Dalhousie, he waved his hands around, he combed his hair and he looked at the wharf. He got down in a boat and he looked up at it. He gave it every possible consideration. It was a sure thing that the government would look after that wharf immediately.
This wharf at Dalhousie had been the subject of many petitions from the mayor of the town, from the warden and members of the municipal council, but nothing had happened. There was an awful lot of stir but nothing happened. This wharf is still inadequate to meet the needs of the shippers. Some time ago I went over and sat down with the minister and asked him what he intended to do. He tried to blame it on the Minister of Public Works. Where do we go with all this? I want results. It should be a simple matter to sit down and state the problem and have it solved, instead of having all this finagling and the making of phony campaign issues out of it, and then end up by doing nothing about this problem.
I have a few remarks to make about the Chignecto canal. This is something that has been batted around ever since confederation. I was talking to an industrialist not long ago who has plans for the area around Saint John, a refinery, smelter and so on. It is unbelievable that the government should refuse to go ahead with the building of the Chignecto canal. This refusal has held back the economy of the maritime provinces all through the years. The building of the Chignecto canal was the basis upon which the Atlantic provinces came into confederation in the first place. In its dying days this government should examine its conscience and take action, belated though it may be. All they have to do is get the machinery rolling. They have the means to do it, and it would be quite simple. I am very much surprised and taken aback with the Prime Minister's insatiable desire to rock and roll the Canadian confederation.
It is high time this government got down on its knees and recognized the seriousness
The Budget-Mr. Van Horne of these problems. We did not enter confederation merely for the purpose of sending representatives to Ottawa to sit around here. Our forefathers entered confederation in the firm belief that we of the maritimes would be treated as equal partners and given equal economic opportunities to develop as we had developed before we entered confederation.
Let me speak about the budget. The hon. member for Dauphin raised a remarkable hypothetical speculation the other day as to how the increase in the old age pensions of $6 per month would work out. The plain truth is that the government is not going to fool anybody; the Liberal party is trying desperately to pick up a few votes. The very fact that this government ignored our older people as the cost of living went up, a terrific increase having taken place since these pensions first went into effect, is just additional evidence of the shameful hypocrisy of the government in its consideration of these people.
And there is nothing in the budget for the working people who shoulder the main burden of taxation in this country. Just before the Liberal convention I went around my constituency, and I found that the people are insulted. They wanted to know what the government was trying to do. They asked me just how silly could the government get. They considered they were being insulted with an increase of $1 a month in family allowances when the cost of living had practically doubled since they went into effect. They wanted to know what they were expected to do with invalid pensions which are cancelled the minute they enter an institution, at the very time they would be most in need of them.
It is time this government, in its dying days, made a careful examination of its conscience and struck its breast the three times necessary to expatiate at least in part its sins for refusing to accept responsibility for these things. I hope I am not using words that might be considered to be out of order. After so much pleading by hon. members of the opposition we are told there will be an increase of $6 per month in the old age pension and $1 per month in the family allowance, with nothing for the working man. Such treatment can only be called, and it is being called from one end of the country to the other, an insult. This budget is an insult and is considered a bribe for votes. Those are strong words, but they are true words.
If these increases are needed now, how much more they were needed a few years

The Budget-Mr. Van Horne ago. Why must the government wait until the eve of an election to reduce the taxation on pop? Why must the government wait for the eve of an election to give $1 more a month for the sake of getting a few votes? The budget is a disappointment, not only to the opposition members but to the vast majority of the members of this house, including the Liberal members. The overriding note is the utter lack of consideration for the wage earners of this country, who are again given the cold shoulder. Any relief from the heavy burden of taxation will have to wait for another day and very possibly another government. These small, puerile increases further incite our people to the sentiments they will express in no uncertain way on the 17th of June.
Mr. Speaker, this sum of $2 million in freight-rate assistance in the maritimes is just another hand-out which does not solve or cure the basic problem of our economic ills in the Atlantic area.
The house was startled yesterday to hear what was done by the Prime Minister, however unintentionally, with regard to the letter written to the C.B.C. I do not want to go over this question again, because it was discussed yesterday; but the point I wish to make is that when one medium of information is controlled partially by the government then all mediums of information risk being equally controlled by the government. It is well known that control of one medium only, means the partial control of all mediums. When I think of reporters being offered all-expense paid trips to Quebec, with the sky the limit, to take in the dinner given for the Prime Minister, I ask what else is that but a covert attempt to control the press? Whether you control the medium at the point of a gun or whether you buy it, the end is still control. That is what is hurting -the country most at this time. Another harmful practice is that of having assignments given on the basis of the popularity of reporters with government officials, which is just another way in which news is controlled. That is well known.
Mr. Speaker, before I sit down I would like to say this very sincerely, repeating what I said when I came here on January 16, 1956. Just give me the chance to say that you are good fellows across the way, and I will do it so quickly you won't know what happened.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Please don't.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It must always be remembered that we are here to do our duty toward

the people we represent. That is the crux of the matter. We are sent here to do a job, and I don't know why any hon. member should come here if he is not prepared to do that job according to the dictates of his conscience. That applies to all our people. We owe that duty not only to those who vote Conservative, but to Liberals and to members of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties who happen to live in our constituencies. I can tell the hon. member for Charlotte that at the provincial hospital in Campbellton very prominent Liberals are given exceptionally good jobs. When coping with problems of poverty, disease and despair, politics do not enter into it; they do not ask what party you belong to.
Mr. Speaker, if only we could come to an understanding in this house that our problems are too great to be treated on a purely partisan basis, that our people suffer too much, and that too many people die in tarpaper shacks for the Minister of Public Works not to get busy changing the housing act. If we could only realize that we are living in a country so potentially rich that there is no need for people to live in tarpaper shacks, then we might already be some distance toward finding a remedy. I have visited some houses where there is no proper floor; only one room, and ten children living in one shack. Yet 300 feet away there may be ample timber available.
Mr. Speaker, there is no reason why there should be situations like this in a country such as ours. Ministers should visit some of these tar-paper shacks and see the orange crates which are used for kitchen cupboards, crates that have nothing in them. And these people have to wait eight weeks for unemployment cheques.

of frequently uncalled-for criticism by the opposition and more particularly, the official opposition.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If I may be allowed to do so, Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat that it would be most unfortunate, to my mind, if in this house any recourse were made to means which are unworthy of men who sit here to represent the Canadian people. Our people are sensible and deserve that their business be dealt with in all seriousness and calm.
At the beginning of my remarks I would like, on behalf of those whom I have the honour to represent, as well as on behalf of all right thinking Canadians, to offer my most hearty congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on the magnificent family budget he has brought down.
In this budget speech the minister announced a considerable surplus. Had he announced a deficit, we would then have seen the members of the opposition rise to com-
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau plain and to accuse the government of poor management of this country's affairs. When governments of the various Canadian provinces announce surpluses, there is unanimous applause. Now to my mind what is good for the provinces is also good for the government of the Canadian nation. How can something which is right for a provincial legislature be wrong for the federal government?
If the government manages to announce surpluses, we must assume that the business of the Canadian people is in good hands and this is all to the credit of the government which looks after those affairs.
These surpluses, which we have enjoyed over a few years, have allowed us to reduce the national debt and, at the same time, to keep paying old age pensions, disabled pensions and family allowances, besides carrying on public works throughout the country.
If we seriously consider the amendment moved by the Conservative party as well as the sub-amendment moved by the C.C.F. party, we find that neither of those parties requests an increase in old age pensions or doubling family allowances. Why have the opposition parties not seen fit to request in this house that family allowances be doubled and old age pension increased substantially?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is because members of the conservative and socialist parties, who go about the country requesting that the rate of family allowances and old age pensions be doubled, are not serious. Why do they not make such requests here where they could really accomplish something? It is because they are not serious.
On the other hand, the federal government, through the Minister of Finance, has done something concrete against the inflation which is threatening our country. Because of the present circumstances, the Canadian government could not substantially reduce the income tax as the majority of Canadians would have liked.
The budget submitted by the Minister of Finance is a serious budget and I call to witness the Ottawa Citizen which had this to say in its editorial on Friday March 15th, 1957, which I translate: "Popular or not, Mr. Harris' budget shows honesty and courage on the part of its author".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the Canadian people are convinced of the wisdom of the minister's
2902	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau budget, this could, in turn, bring excellent results, even of a political nature, to the government which submitted it.
As I said a while ago, the Minister of Finance submitted a family budget. He increased family allowances to an extent that will cost an extra $42 million to this country. This money will be distributed in the various provinces, to help the Canadian family. He increased old age pensions by $6 a month. Like all members and all Canadians, I would have preferred to see old age pensions raised to $50 or $60 a month. However, the increase of $6 a month represents an expenditure of approximately $70 million a year.
The government also raised veterans pensions and allowances.
It has also granted a $100 exemption for charitable donations and medical costs, for which vouchers will no longer be needed, and, according to experts, approximately 125,000 Canadian families will benefit by it.
I have listened with great attention during the budget debate to the various members of the opposition parties making all sorts of suggestions in this house and I have come to the conclusion that, if all those suggestions had been accepted, it would have been necessary to double and even treble the Canadian budget and, accordingly to double and treble taxes.
We have a sound budget. The Minister of Finance has given us an excellent budget.
In closing these few remarks I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Finance as well as to this house. At the beginning of this session, the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) submitted a resolution and, as I fear that it will not be considered before the end of this session, I should like to read that proposition and to make a suggestion to the government. Here it is:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the income tax act so as to provide for the exemption from income taxes of tuition fees paid to universities, vocational training schools, military colleges, academies and other institutions of higher learning, as well as the cost to students of all textbooks and scientific equipment necessary to the courses followed in these institutions of learning.
I congratulate the hon. member for Cartier for inserting that resolution in the orders of the day and I support him wholeheartedly.
I had the opportunity during this session of expressing my views on different matters concerning education and training in Canada as a whole as well as in our different provinces. If the government decided to adopt that resolution, we could thus contribute to the


education and training of our young people, according to the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution. We would be helping those students who, in increasing number, want to get an education and add to our national heritage. We would be helping also a large number of fathers and mothers who make heavy sacrifices in order to give an education to their children. I think the government should give serious consideration to that resolution.
As I was saying a moment ago the government has introduced a sound budget. On the eve of a general election, before going to the people, the government could of course have reduced taxes as a vote-getting device. But the Liberal party with the record it has does not have to use such methods to be returned to power. It will be returned on its record, its political past and its achievements. The government in power has practised a national policy and has ensured prosperity.
According to the hon. member who spoke before me, the government should develop our national resources. Well, to answer the hon. member I think that the people of this country have seen the government develop our national resources to the benefit of the Canadian people as a whole. Never has the standard of living in this country been as high as it is now. If we now enjoy this prosperity, whose benefits extend to every Canadian family, it is because the administration of this country is in the hands of a government that looks to the sound management of its business. When the hon. member makes remarks of that kind I feel I must point out to him that he is facing a government which provides proof to the contrary. When we go to the people, in the very near future, I am convinced that they will renew this government's mandate because it works in the interest of Canada and of Canadians.
While the government is working in the interests of this country and looking after its business, the opposition-and this has been the case for the last four years-has been making frequent unjustified criticism without suggesting anything concrete to the government.
As I was saying a moment ago I am convinced that feeling sure as I do of the gratitude of the Canadian people who have given close attention to the achievements of the government in power, this government will be returned with a large majority in the next general elections, on its record and its achievements.

Now, Mr. Speaker, we have had an opportunity of becoming acquainted in the course of the last few days with the Fowler commission report. In the first speech I had occasion to deliver in this house, I had referred to the problems facing the C.B.C. and these problems have seemed to me to be highly important, for a long time. Such being the case I might recall that on the 28th of January 1955, in the debate on the address in reply I stated that I was fully in accord with certain groups who claimed that the C.B.C. operated in competition with private stations and that it should therefore not be up to it to decide to whom licenses should be given for radio or television stations. I was glad to note that the Fowler commission, in its report, recommended the establishment of a board of governors of television and radio broadcasting which would have jurisdiction over private and public broadcasting although the board would be answerable to parliament.
I know that the report of that commission is but a recommendation to the government but I hope that, in the near future, next year or at least as soon as possible, these recommendations will be implemented by the government as I believe that they would serve not only the interest of radio and television broadcasting, but also the interests of this country.
In that same report, it is recommended that the federal treasury should contribute about $470 million during the next six years to finance the expansion and maintenance of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and in particular of the television services.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was established, some years ago, to promote Canadian culture in this country. In my opinion, it is very important to appropriate large sums of money to promote the expansion of a purely Canadian culture. The Fowler commission, in its report, gives the following definition of Canadian culture:
The progress of Canadian culture is not the privilege of a few. It must comprise all Canadian ways of living and offer opportunities to all citizens.
The Fowler commission believes that such a definition is accurate and that national broadcasting must constantly strive to achieve it. All those forms of culture must be part of the minimum of national radio and television broadcasting services and, except under unusual circumstances, all stations, public and private, of the network involved should make full use of these services.
And that is why I wholeheartedly support the recommendation of the Fowler commission that a huge amount be spent on the
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau expansion of radio and television in this country. Also, if we want to encourage the formation of a Canadian culture, I think that another recommendation of that same commission should be adopted. This recommendation is to the effect that we should not allow more than 20 per cent of the shares to fall into the hands of outsiders.
The Fowler commission's report forecasts that the broadcasting of colour TV will be achieved within two years. Television is a terrific medium for advertising. Furthermore, it is proposed to improve the services of the C.B.C. which does already an excellent job, and this will benefit the Canadian people.
I am grateful to the government authorities for the great help they have so generously given me during my whole term of office, which enabled me to serve my fellow citizens, and more particularly those of Dollard county, which I am proud to represent in this house. For the last few years, I have, in this parliament of Canada, contributed to the working out of various legislation, as it is indeed the first and foremost duty of a people's representative. I did so with a view to serve my fellow-citizens from sea to sea. Thanks to the co-operation of the government, I was able more particularly to help my fellow-citizens from the county of Dollard. As a matter of fact, as it became necessary, the building of a post-office at Youville was carried out. Moreover, the erection of another post-office in Ville St. Laurent will soon begin, which will answer the urgent need of the local population. As the minister is occupying his seat, I seize this opportunity to thank him very sincerely on behalf of the people of Dollard county. He has shown great understanding towards the people. I thank him for so generously considering the request I made to him on that matter, a request which I have renewed many times.
I would feel remiss if I did not thank the government for putting up the splendid building where the offices of the National Film Board are now located in the county of Dollard. The population of my riding is proud and glad of that fact.
I had also the privilege, thanks to the co-operation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), of obtaining the installation of warning devices at many level crossings in the county of Dollard. Negotiations are underway for the construction of a viaduct on Decarie boulevard. I have every reason to believe that this project will be implemented in the near future.

The Address-Mr. Pearkes
I thank the government which, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), has granted some assistance to Notre-Dame-de-l'Esperance hospital in Ville St. Laurent.
Thanks to the close co-operation of the government as a whole, and of each one of its members in particular, it was possible to achieve something favourable for the people of Dollard county.
In concluding my remarks I shall thank the hon. Minister of Finance again (Mr. Harris) for introducing a favourable family budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon at the conclusion of the remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer I indicated my desire to address some remarks of my own on the same subject, but the Minister of Finance then indicated that he had to leave the house. It was either a question of adjourning the debate at that time or allowing discussion of that particular subject to continue in the budget debate; therefore I am going to take this opportunity of referring to the remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer.
The hon. member had suggested that some form of commission might be established in order to ascertain whether the defence estimates could not be reduced, and whether it is necessary to spend more than about 60 per cent of what is being spent today in order to get the same type of defence protection. He emphasized the point that he believed in the necessity for having adequate defence forces, but he had previously said there was plenty of evidence to indicate that there was duplication and unnecessary expense. He recommended that there be some clamping down on defence expenditure.
While I feel it is necessary to review our defence expenditures, I cannot agree with the thought that there can be a reduction of 40 per cent in order to meet his requirement. I do feel that the changing world situation still makes it essential that we maintain adequate forces, and with the introduction of the many new weapons which are now being produced by scientists the world over I do not see how there can be any substantial reduction in the amount Canada is paying for her defence for some considerable time.
This does not mean that I believe all the money which is being spent for defence is going to the forces or for the type of weapons they need so urgently. In fact we will have to consider the distribution of the defence vote

in order to see not only that the taxpayer gets full value for the money that is voted, but also to ensure that the troops themselves get the weapons which are so essential if they are to be given a fighting chance should there be a war in the future. I feel that our whole effort must be the maintenance of peace. This, of course, is axiomatic. At the present time we can only ensure peace through strength, and I think we must adhere to that axiom just as much as we adhere to our desire for peace.
During the past few months our attention has been focused on the rapidly changing conditions in the Middle East. From week to week plans have been made by the United Nations which have had to be changed or modified to meet an ever-varying situation. Our own Canadian troops, army, navy and air force, have played a very practical part in putting into effect the policies of the United Nations with the result that, perhaps with the exception of those tragic events which happened in Hungary, comparatively little attention has been paid to what has been going on in other parts of the world. In any event, the concentration upon the events which have happened in the Middle East has, I think, obscured the far-reaching changes that have taken place, and are still taking place, in the relative strengths of the two great power blocs, the east and the west.
Although there have been changes in the personnel in the Kremlin, and although from time to time honeyed words have been spoken, there appears to be very little change in the over-all desire of the Russians to achieve the objectives which they set out many years ago. The small reductions in armed forces which Russia announced a year ago really have done nothing to reduce the power of the Russian military machine. Really the reductions have been far more a process of streamlining than any step toward disarmament. It was only about a week ago that the Russian government signed an agreement with East Germany to retain 20 Russian divisions in East Germany.
We have, I think, been lulled into believing that the forces which NATO has assembled in Europe are an adequate shield against this threat which may be developing in the east. But these NATO forces now stationed in Europe have been greatly reduced of late. As you know, France has had to reduce the number of her troops in Europe forming part of that NATO shield in order to send soldiers to North Africa. Great Britain is in the process of making radical reductions in her force, which was something over 70,000 men,

to one which it is contemplated will not exceed 50,000. The British hope to effect this reduction by reducing the number of administrative units rather than front-line troops. The whole trend seems to be toward more flexible units with greater Are power, which would indicate the type of force of the future.
No longer is the division, as it was known in the first and second war, to be considered the basic formation. The division is now to be replaced by small, self-contained brigades or regimental groups consisting of three infantry batallions, an armoured regiment and an artillery regiment with small signal, medical and other units attached. The divisional supply column, with that long train we used to know, is now a thing of the past. For a number of years it has been considered that the nuclear bombs held by the United States air force would constitute a deterrent and that Russia would never attempt another global war. It was felt that the light shield of NATO troops in Europe would be sufficient to block any movement of ground forces across western Europe.
While the possibility that Russia might attack this continent had been recognized, it has until now been felt that Russia would hardly dare to initiate such an attack for fear of instant retaliation which would follow both by the United States strategic bomber forces and the British medium bombers.
On January 9 of this year, speaking in this house, the Prime Minister-his remarks can be found at page 33 of Hansard-indicated that he felt that if the aggressors did attack, Canada would be in the path of any such attack directed against the United States, and he expressed the intention to make that path as difficult and dangerous as possible for the aggressors to follow. These are sentiments which are perfectly acceptable. One may question whether Canada has taken adequate steps to safeguard the residents of her country against the possibility of such a path being followed, but that statement does assume that those behind the iron curtain will be the aggressor, and that the attack will develop across the north pole, to be met by the inevitable retaliation which he hoped would be carried out with as great damage to the aggressor as he might cause to us; the inference, of course, being that the enemy is to make the decision as to whether or not he will attack with nuclear bombs.
However, I suggest that the world situation has changed now to the extent that it is unlikely that the Russians would, as the
The Address-Mr. Pearkes first phase of a war, attempt to carry out a nuclear attack upon this country. They are far more likely-and I can support my contention by remarks from the highest British authorities, including Field Marshal Montgomery-now to take advantage of the weakening of the NATO shield in western Europe and move through Europe with their ground forces. It is very doubtful whether they would at that time use their nuclear weapons. Our NATO forces have been reduced to a very serious extent, so that if Russia does not use her nuclear bombs in the first instance, then either the United States or Great Britain will be faced with that awful decision as to whether they will start the massive retaliation, and will be the first nation to use the nuclear weapons.
The British army and, to certainly a lesser extent, our own Canadian army are now having developed atomic warheads for some of their artillery and their new weapons. In fact it is only by having the most up to date weapons for use by the ground forces and to be employed in Europe that we could ever have a hope of checking the large Russian numbers, unless the nuclear bomb was used.
I	think as the use of nuclear bombs is bound to meet with retaliation, no matter who uses them first, because the Russians are fast reaching parity with the west in their supply of nuclear weapons, then it would practically mean a suicidal war for both sides.
I think, Mr. Speaker, at this point you might call it six o'clock. I move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Pearkes the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave I move:
That on Wednesday, April 3, 1957, and on every Wednesday thereafter until the end of this session the hours of sitting shall be 2.30 to 10 p.m.; that on Thursday, April 4 next, and on every Monday, Tuesday and Thursday thereafter until the end of this session, the hours of sitting shall be from
II	a.m. until 10 p.m.; there shall be the usual intermissions at 1 and 6 p.m.; and that the provisions of standing orders 2(1) and 6(1) and (3) be suspended in relation thereto.

Business of the House

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: WEDNESDAY EVENING AND MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one does have to look at motions such as this and make sure that we are not imposing too much of an additional burden on the members of our staff; but because we believe we are adding these extra hours for only a couple of weeks we are prepared to agree to the motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: WEDNESDAY EVENING AND MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext: I can tell the hon. gentleman that those of us who are in charge of the administration always take all these matters into consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: WEDNESDAY EVENING AND MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext: But it is the house that passes these motions, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: WEDNESDAY EVENING AND MORNING SITTINGS
speechtext:
We always submit to the
house that, in consideration of the hours imposed by the house on itself, certain alleviations in staff working conditions be made. Since I know the feelings of the hon. gentleman and the feelings of other hon. members, they always accede to the request made in that direction.
May I immediately submit to the house that whenever we have adopted these hours it
has always been our practice in the past to split the working hours for the page boys. Some of them are on duty in the morning and those who come in the morning do not come in the afternoon; they come in the evening. When a new schedule is worked out I shall ask hon. members whether they agree that the splitting of the hours schedule that has been adopted in the past shall be followed again. I take it we shall have the approval of the house in that regard.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speechtext: I have another matter to mention before I announce the adjournment. On Monday a bit of history will be made in this house, in that a lady will come to the house as a Hansard reporter. She is Mrs. Joan C. Blair, who has worked as a Hansard reporter in the legislature of Ontario, where I am told one has been working in that capacity for the last three years. I am sure the house will by its applause welcome, as it is convenient, the entrance of this first lady Hansard reporter in the house on Monday.
